York's population increased by around 4,800 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 200,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of York increased by 2.4%, from just under 198,100 in 2011 to around 202,800 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of Yorkshire and The Humber (3.7%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, York was home to around 5.3 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 5.2 in 2011. This area was close to the median population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in York than across Yorkshire and The Humber

Median age in York

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of York increased by one year, from 38 to 39 years of age.

This area had a slightly lower average (median) age than Yorkshire and The Humber as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a slightly lower average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by just over 3,300 (an increase of 19.7%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 3,600 (9.0% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 1.4 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Disability in York

York saw Yorkshire and The Humber's largest percentage-point rise in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 9.5% in 2011 to 10.9% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Ryedale saw Yorkshire and The Humber's next largest increase in the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little (from 9.1% in 2011 to 10.0% in 2021).

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the proportion of residents who were identified as disabled and limited a little increased from 10.5% to 10.7%, while the proportion in nearby Selby increased from 9.6% to 9.9%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a little in York increased by 1.4 percentage points

Health in York

In 2021, 48.5% of York residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 47.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" rose from 34.7% to 35.0%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of York residents describing their health as "very bad" was 0.9% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" was 3.4% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in York increased by 0.6 percentage points

Unpaid care in York

In 2021, 4.6% of York residents (aged five years and over) reported providing up to 19 hours of unpaid care each week. This figure decreased from 7.2% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The decrease in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in York (2.6 percentage points) was similar to the decrease across Yorkshire and The Humber (2.7 percentage points, from 7.1% to 4.4%). Across England, the proportion fell by 2.8 percentage points, from 7.2% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in York decreased by 2.6 percentage points

Religion in York

In 2021, 46.1% of York residents reported having "No religion", making it the most common response in this local authority area (up from 30.1% in 2011). Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 25.9% to 39.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 43.9% of people in York described themselves as Christian (down from 59.5%), while 6.9% did not state their religion (down from 7.8% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 46.1% of usual residents in York reported having "No religion"

Fall in employment

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were employed was greater in York (3.0 percentage points) than across England (0.8 percentage points).

In York, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) decreased from 55.5% in 2011 to 52.5% in 2021. During the same period, the percentage across England decreased from 56.5% to 55.7%.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in York fell from 2.8% to 1.8%, while the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were retired (economically inactive) increased from 21.8% to 22.5%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were employed (excluding full-time students) in York decreased by 3.0 percentage points

Change in work hours

In 2021, 12.5% of York residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 11.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 1 in 11 people (9.2%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 11.2% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 56.0% to 56.9%.

This area had the region’s highest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week. Craven had Yorkshire and The Humber's next highest percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week (12.3%), while Wakefield had the region's lowest percentage (7.9%).

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in York increased by 0.8 percentage points

York residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 174,600 York residents said they were born in England. This represented 86.1% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 173,000 in 2011, which at the time represented 87.3% of York's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with around 3,800 York residents reporting this country of birth (1.9%). This figure was down from around 4,300 in 2011, which at the time represented 2.2% of the population of York.

The number of York residents born in China rose from just over 1,400 in 2011 (0.7% of the local population) to around 2,000 in 2021 (1.0%).

In 2021, 86.1% of York residents reported their country of birth as England

Lone parents in York

In 2021, 8.6% of York households included a lone parent. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (8.7%).

York saw Yorkshire and The Humber's joint third-largest fall (alongside Harrogate) in the percentage of lone-parent households. This area had the region’s seventh lowest percentage of lone-parent households.

The percentage of households including a lone parent in York decreased by 0.1 percentage points

Relationships in York

In 2021, 8.4% of York residents (aged 16 years and over) said they had got divorced or dissolved a civil partnership. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (8.5%).

In 2021, just over 4 in 10 people (41.3%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 44.3% in 2011. The percentage of adults who were never married or in a civil partnership in York increased from 38.6% to 42.8%.

York saw Yorkshire and The Humber's joint third-largest fall (alongside Sheffield and Wakefield) in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership. This area had the region’s third lowest percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in York decreased by 0.1 percentage points

National identity in York

In 2021, 7.2% of York residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 6.2% in 2011.

In 2021, just over 1 in 50 people (2.1%) identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.7% in 2011. The percentage of residents in York that identified as "British only" increased from 17.3% to 56.4%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.6 percentage points, from 5.1% to 6.7%) than in York (1.0 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in York increased by 1.0 percentage points

Change in housing in York

Of York households, 65.1% owned their home in 2021, down from 66.1% in 2011.

In 2021, around one in five households (20.0%) rented privately, compared with 17.9% in 2011. The percentage of York households that lived in a socially rented property remained at 14.0%.

The decrease in the percentage of households that owned their home was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.5 percentage points, from 64.1% to 62.6%) than in York (1.0 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 2.0 percentage points, from 63.3% to 61.3%.

The rate of home ownership in York decreased by 1.0 percentage points

Ethnic groups in York

In 2021, 1.8% of York residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 1.2% in 2011. The 0.6 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.6% to 2.1%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 92.8% of people in York identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 94.3% in 2011), while 3.8% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (compared with 3.4% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.5% in 2011 to 1.0% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
